title: Designing a hand warmer or cold pack
keyIdea: A hand warmer uses an exothermic change, which transfers energy to the surroundings so the temperature rises. A cold pack uses an endothermic change, which takes in energy from the surroundings so the temperature falls. To design one, test which substance gives a big enough change in the right direction, change one variable at a time in a fair test, tune the amount to reach a safe temperature, and insulate the pack so the energy transfer is slower and the effect lasts longer.

kid: Some solids warm the water they dissolve in. Calcium chloride does this. The change gives energy out to the water, so the temperature goes up. We call it exothermic. That is what a hand warmer needs.

Other solids cool the water. Ammonium nitrate does this. The change takes energy in from the water, so the temperature goes down. We call it endothermic. That is what a cold pack needs. Cold does not flow in. Energy flows out of the water.

To pick the best solid, test each one the same way. Use the same mass, the same volume of water and the same start temperature. Change one thing at a time, and measure the start and end temperature. Then you know what caused the change.

More solid gives a bigger change, so the amount matters. Too little and the pack does nothing. Too much and it could burn or freeze skin. A good hand warmer stays below about 45 °C. Packs cool down or warm up again as energy spreads to the air. Wrapping a pack in felt slows that down, because felt traps air and air is a poor conductor. So the pack keeps working for longer.
adult: This lesson matches NGSS MS-PS1-6. Learners design, build and test a device that gives out or takes in thermal energy through a chemical process. It also fits the work on exothermic and endothermic changes in KS3 and GCSE chemistry in England. The lab uses four solids that dissolve in water: calcium chloride, ammonium nitrate, ammonium chloride and sodium chloride.

Key terms: exothermic, endothermic, energy transfer, surroundings, temperature change, fair test, and the independent, dependent and control variables. Also insulation and thermal conductivity. The lab's numbers come from each solid's energy change on dissolving, shared by 50 g of water with no heat lost. That gives about 3.5 °C per gram for calcium chloride and −1.5 °C per gram for ammonium nitrate. Real results are a bit smaller, as some energy escapes.

Common mistakes: saying cold flows into the water, when energy flows out of it; calling any temperature change exothermic; changing two things at once; and thinking more water gives a bigger change. In fact more water spreads the same energy over more mass. Some think insulation makes more energy, when it only slows the transfer.

Real products use the same ideas. Throwaway warmers use iron powder rusting, gel warmers use sodium acetate as it turns solid, and cold packs dissolve ammonium nitrate or urea. Ammonium nitrate is an oxidiser and calcium chloride stings eyes, so wear eye protection. In the lab the learner tests four solids, matches them to briefs, runs a fair test, tunes the mass and picks a sleeve.

familyTip: Hold a reusable gel hand warmer, or a bag of frozen peas, and ask which way the energy is moving: into your hand or out of it. Then wrap one in a tea towel and compare how long it lasts with one left bare.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: test four solids in water, pick one for each brief, run a fair test, tune the mass to a safe temperature, then insulate the pack.

practice.prompt: You need an instant cold pack for a sprained ankle. Which kind of change should it use?
choices: An endothermic change, which takes in energy from the surroundings
An exothermic change, which gives out energy
A change with no energy transfer
practice.hint: The pack must get colder. Which way must the energy move?
practice.explain: A cold pack takes energy in from the ankle and the air around it, so it is endothermic. Dissolving ammonium nitrate in water is a common example.

practice.prompt: Water starts at 20 °C. After a solid dissolves it is at {t} °C. By how many degrees did the temperature rise?
practice.hint: Temperature change = end temperature − start temperature.
practice.explain: {t} − 20 = {=t-20} °C. The temperature went up, so the change is exothermic.

practice.prompt: In a test, each gram of calcium chloride raised the temperature of 50 cm³ of water by 3.5 °C. Water starts at 20 °C. What end temperature do you expect with {m} g, in the same water?
practice.hint: Multiply the change per gram by the number of grams, then add it to the start temperature.
practice.explain: Rise = {m} × 3.5 = {=3.5*m} °C, so the end temperature is 20 + {=3.5*m} = {=20+3.5*m} °C.

practice.prompt: Mia tests whether more calcium chloride gives a bigger rise. Cup B has twice the solid and also twice the water. What is wrong with her test?
choices: Two variables changed, so she cannot tell which one caused the result
Nothing: more of everything makes it fairer
She should have used a different solid in cup B
practice.hint: In a fair test, how many things should be different between the cups?
practice.explain: Only the variable being tested, the mass, should change. Twice the water spreads the energy over more mass, which hides the effect of the extra solid.

pool.prompt: Ammonium nitrate dissolves in water and the water gets colder. What happened?
choices: Energy was transferred from the water into the dissolving, so it is endothermic
The solid gave out cold, so it is exothermic
No energy moved; the water just changed
pool.hint: Cold is not a substance. Think about which way energy moved.
pool.explain: The temperature fell because energy left the water and was taken in by the dissolving process. Taking in energy from the surroundings is endothermic.

pool.prompt: Which result would make the best hand warmer?
choices: A solid that raised the water from 20 °C to 42 °C
A solid that lowered the water from 20 °C to 12 °C
A solid that raised the water from 20 °C to 21 °C
pool.hint: A hand warmer needs the right direction of change and a big enough change.
pool.explain: A rise of 22 °C is exothermic and large enough to warm hands, while staying below about 45 °C. A 1 °C rise is too small, and a fall is the wrong direction.

pool.prompt: 5 g of a solid raised the temperature of some water by {d} °C. About how much would 10 g raise the same amount of water by, in °C?
pool.hint: Twice the solid releases about twice the energy into the same water.
pool.explain: Double the mass gives about double the energy, so the rise is about 2 × {d} = {=2*d} °C.

pool.prompt: You compare two cold-pack mixes. Which must you keep the same?
choices: The mass of solid, the volume of water and the start temperature
Only the type of solid
Nothing, as long as you measure carefully
pool.hint: Only the thing you are testing, the type of solid, should change.
pool.explain: The type of solid is the independent variable. Mass, water volume, start temperature and container are control variables, so any difference in temperature change is caused by the solid.

pool.prompt: A hand warmer cools down too quickly. Which change helps most?
choices: Put it inside a felt sleeve
Use a thinner plastic bag
Add more water to the same amount of solid
pool.hint: Which change slows the energy transfer to the air?
pool.explain: Felt traps air, which is a poor thermal conductor, so energy leaves the pack more slowly and it stays warm longer. More water would make the rise smaller.

pool.prompt: Each gram of ammonium nitrate lowers the temperature of 50 cm³ of water by 1.5 °C. Water starts at 20 °C. What end temperature do you expect with {m} g?
pool.hint: Work out the total drop, then take it away from 20 °C.
pool.explain: Drop = {m} × 1.5 = {=1.5*m} °C, so the end temperature is 20 − {=1.5*m} = {=20-1.5*m} °C.

pool.prompt: A reusable hand warmer gets warm when the liquid inside crystallises. What kind of change is the crystallising?
choices: Exothermic
Endothermic
Neither: there is no energy change
pool.hint: The pack gets warmer. Is energy given out or taken in?
pool.explain: Sodium acetate releases energy to the surroundings as it crystallises, so the change is exothermic. Boiling the pack later puts that energy back in.

pool.prompt: A cold pack design only cools by 2 °C. What is the best next step?
choices: Test it again with more solid in the same water
Use twice as much water
Give up, because no cold pack can be improved
pool.hint: Which change gives the dissolving more energy to take in from the water?
pool.explain: More solid takes in more energy, so the drop gets bigger. More water spreads the same energy change over more mass, which makes the drop smaller.
